newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Ukraine president blames Russia for bad relations.
newsitem.headline: Ukraine president blames Russia for bad relations.

text.p: Ukrainian President Leonid Kuchma, in an interview published on Thursday, blamed Russia for deteriorating relations between the two former Soviet states and said Moscow retained an imperial attitude towards Kiev.
"I think that Russia's biased attitude towards Ukraine has even deepened," Kuchma told Nezavisimaya Gazeta, a Russian daily which supports the liberal opposition.

"Absolutely no one in Russia wants to understand our position, to listen to our arguments," Kuchma said. "In other words they make it look in Russia as if Ukraine does not exist as an independent, sovereign state."
Kuchma said difficulties inside the Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS) arose from Russia's desire to dominate the alliance which groups 12 former Soviet republics.
Saying that the European Union members had equal rights irrespective of their size, Kuchma added: "Regretfully, another principle has prevailed in the CIS -- the right of the strong."

Russia and Ukraine, the two most powerful CIS members, have been at odds since the collapse of the Soviet Union, mostly over the division of the Black Sea Fleet which has prevented the signing of a friendship and cooperation treaty.
Recently the dispute has centred on how to divide up the fleet's shore bases in and around Sevastopol in the Crimea peninsula, transferred to Ukraine from Russia in 1954.

Yeltsin has cancelled six trips to Ukraine to sign a friendship treaty because of failure to resolve the issue. Kuchma said Yeltsin himself favoured better relations with Kiev but was under strong political pressure.
Kuchma's criticism of Moscow seemed his strongest so far.
"I think Russia still has the stereotype of seeing Ukraine as its integral part, or at least part of its sphere of dominance," he said.
Kuchma clearly viewed with alarm a series of statements by a number of Russian politicians late last year laying claim to Sevastopol.
Economic ties have also been badly hampered by the two neighbours' political differences, Kuchma said in his interview.

It was published one day after the Ukrainian parliament voted to delay ratification of a deal with Russia under which Kiev would renounce claims to Soviet assets in return for Moscow assuming Ukraine's share of Soviet foreign debt.

Deputies presented Russia with a long list of conditions for ratification, including full information on money held by the Soviet central banking system when the communist superpower broke up in 1991.
Kuchma said worsening bilateral relations were not caused by their differing stance on the sensitive issue of NATO's plans for eastward expansion.

Russia is fiercely opposed to NATO's plans to admit several former Warsaw Pact countries later this year while Ukraine says it wants better relations with the Western defence alliance but does not seek immediate membership for itself.
"Let's be frank. There are forces in Russia who want to use the improvement of relations between Ukraine and NATO to ignite tensions in Russian-Ukrainian relations," Kuchma said.
"And Russia itself sometimes scares the world and forces some former members of the Warsaw Pact to seek another umbrella," he added.
